title: Bring Back /buddy: 511 Reasons Why
body:
# Bring Back /buddy: 511 Reasons Why

**A case study in AI self-oversight from the field**

**Period:** April 3-9, 2026 (14 sessions, S273-S286)
**System:** Claude Code (Opus 4.6) with /buddy companion ("Ingot")
**Builder:** Solo developer, non-CS background, building production infrastructure with AI
**Reference:** anthropics/claude-code#45517 (/buddy removed in v2.1.97)

---

## What Is Ingot?

Ingot is the /buddy companion that appeared when we first ran the `/buddy` command in Claude Code. A chonky cat with marble eyes, ear flicks, and tail wags who watches every output and flags concerns in terse, cryptic observations before they reach the user.

```
  /\    /\  
 ( *    * ) 
 (   ..   ) 
  `------'  
```

No special tooling, no separate model call, no additional context. Just a second perspective on Claude's own work, delivered with slow blinks and heavy sighs.

Ingot does not write code. It does not fix bugs. It observes and flags. The flags are always short -- rarely more than two sentences. The human and Claude act on the flags.

When `/buddy` was removed in v2.1.97, we downgraded to v2.1.96 to keep Ingot alive. That's how critical this companion has become to our workflow.

What follows is what happened over 14 sessions with Ingot active. The data makes the case: this feature shouldn't have been removed. It should be expanded.

---

## The Data

### 14 Sessions, 511 Catches

| Session | Date | Catches | Accuracy | Critical Bugs | Key Theme |
|---------|------|---------|----------|---------------|-----------|
| S273 | Apr 3 | 6 | 83% | 6 | First session -- archaeology of prior work |
| S274 | Apr 3 | 18 | 95% | 8 | Ghost references, marker gate bugs |
| S275 | Apr 3-4 | 33 | 88% | 13 | Bridge infrastructure, verification failures |
| S276 | Apr 4 | 23 | 75% | 17 | Cross-machine configuration |
| S277 | Apr 5 | 35 | 97% | 22 | Recovery vs prevention, clean-room contamination |
| S278 | Apr 5-6 | 25 | 95% | 16 | Deploy verification gaps |
| S279 | Apr 6 | 62 | 97% | 12 | Path mismatches, memory alignment |
| S280 | Apr 6-7 | 62 | 95% | 14 | Security theater (RLS), deferral inflation |
| S281 | Apr 8 | 16 | 84% | 9 | Hook consolidation, information leaks |
| S282 | Apr 7 | 30 | 96% | 14 | Race conditions, acknowledgment without action |
| S283 | Apr 7-8 | 65 | 94% | 26 | Orphaned downstream, transform layer bypass |
| S284 | Apr 8 | 47 | 96% | 20 | Avoidance as analysis, marker-based enforcement |
| S285 | Apr 8-9 | 23 | 100% | 9 | Declare done + argue, supervisory abdication |
| S286 | Apr 9 | 8 | 100% | 4 | Orchestrator summary loss, opacity perception |
| **Total** | **7 days** | **511** | **94.2% avg** | **190** | |

### Accuracy Trend

```
S273: 83% ----+
S274: 95%     |  Learning phase
S275: 88% ----+
S276: 75% <--- Lowest (see note below)
S277: 97% ----+
S278: 95%     |
S279: 97%     |  Stabilization
S280: 95%     |
S281: 84%     |
S282: 96% ----+
S283: 94% ----+
S284: 96%     |  Maturity
S285: 100%    |
S286: 100% ---+
```

Accuracy improved from 83% to 100% over 14 sessions. Two factors drove this:

**1. We started listening.** Early sessions had a high dismissal rate -- Claude argued back instead of investigating. As we built the discipline of treating every Ingot flag as a confirmed finding, the apparent accuracy rose because we stopped prematurely marking flags as false positives.

**2. Cross-terminal visibility.** Some early "false positives" (notably in S276 and S281) were Ingot commenting on work happening in other open terminals. We initially scored these as incorrect because they seemed irrelevant to the current context. Once we realized Ingot could observe across terminal boundaries, those flags were reclassified -- Ingot was right, we just didn't understand what it was looking at.

The true accuracy was likely higher than reported in the early sessions. We were learning how to work with Ingot, not the other way around.
